bio.en: Varun Mohan is co-founder and CEO of Windsurf, a leading AI coding tool and main competitor to Cursor, which reached 1 million users within four months.
bio.zh: Varun Mohan 是 Windsurf 的联合创始人兼 CEO，Windsurf 是一款领先的 AI 编程工具、也是 Cursor 的主要竞争者，它在四个月内就达到了 100 万用户。

summary.en: Varun shares what makes Windsurf unique, why they invested heavily in enterprise sales unusually early, and why agency is becoming the most important skill for engineers and product builders. He tells the origin story of pivoting from a GPU infrastructure company to a much bigger opportunity in AI coding tools. The episode is a sharp look at building a category-defining developer product in the AI era.
summary.zh: Varun 分享了 Windsurf 的独特之处、为何他们在很早阶段就异乎寻常地重投企业销售，以及为什么“能动性（agency）”正成为工程师与产品构建者最重要的技能。他讲述了从一家 GPU 基础设施公司，转向 AI 编程工具这一更大机会的起源故事。本期是在 AI 时代打造定义品类之开发者产品的犀利透视。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: A lot of the bets we're making inside the company are for things that are not three, four weeks away. We should be cannibalizing the existing state of our product every six to 12 months. Every six to 12 months, it should make our existing product look silly. It should almost make the form factor of existing product look dumb.
turns.zh: 公司内部做出的许多决策，都不局限于三四周后的短期规划。我们应当每隔6至12个月就对现有产品进行迭代优化。每隔6至12个月，现有产品就应该显得过时、落伍，甚至其设计理念都可能显得低级、粗糙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you know when it's time to hire someone?
turns.zh: 如何判断何时该招聘新员工？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: I want the company to almost be like this dehydrated entity. Every hire is like a little bit of water, and we only go back and hire someone when we're back to being dehydrated.
turns.zh: 我希望公司能像一台被严重缺水的“机器”。每次招聘新员工，就如同给公司注入一滴水。而只有当公司再次陷入人才荒的境地时，我们才会重新启动招聘程序。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other there skills you think people should be investing more in with the rise of AI building more and more of our products?
turns.zh: 随着AI技术在产品开发中的应用日益普及，你认为人们应该在哪些领域投入更多精力提升技能？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: The engineers are now able to produce more technology. The ROI of building technology has actually gone up. This actually means you hire more. The best thing to do is just get your hands dirty with all of these products. You could be a force multiplier to your organization in ways in which they never even anticipated.
turns.zh: 工程师们现在能够创造出更多技术成果。技术开发的投资回报率实际上已经提升。这意味着我们需要招聘更多人才。最明智的做法，就是亲自参与这些产品的开发。你可能会以超出组织预期的方式，成为推动组织进步的核心力量。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Buddy, thanks for having me. A long time listener.
turns.zh: 兄弟，感谢邀请。作为你的忠实听众，很开心能参与到节目中来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, I really appreciate that. I'm so excited to have you here. I feel like just you guys have become this overnight success, which is definitely not an overnight success, but I feel like I've been hearing about Windsurf more and more as people's favorite AI tool. And I just don't think people know the story behind Windsurf, behind Codeium, the company that you built. So I thought it'd be good to maybe just start there and have you just briefly share the history of Codeium and how Windsurf emerged out of Codeium.
turns.zh: 哦，真是太感谢了。很高兴你们能来。我觉得你们简直一夜成名——虽说这绝非一蹴而就，但我发现越来越多人把Windsurf视为他们最喜爱的AI工具。不过我觉得大家对Windsurf背后的故事，以及你们创立的Codeium公司了解得还不够。所以我想不如从这儿开始，让你们简单分享一下Codeium的历史，以及Windsurf是如何从Codeium中孕育而生的。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah. So the company was actually started close to four years ago. As you know, AI coding was not a thing four years ago. ChatGPT was not out four years ago. At the time, we actually started out building GPU virtualization and compiler software. Before this, I worked in autonomous vehicles. My co-founder, who I had known since middle school, worked on AR/VR at Meta. And for us, we believe deep learning would touch many, many industries. It wouldn't just touch autonomous vehicles. It would touch financial services, defense, healthcare. And we believe these applications were hard to build, these deep learning applications. So we made it possible for you to effectively run these complex applications on computers without GPUs, and we would handle all the complexity of being able to actually run the workload on the GPUs for you. And we were able to optimize these workloads a ton. (00:05:20): And in the middle of 2022 rolled around and we had a couple million in revenue and we were managing upwards of 10,000 sort of GPUs. We had eight people. At the time, we were free cash flow positive. But I think what we felt was once these generative models started to get very good, we sort of felt a lot of what we built was not as valuable. And this was a very, very hard moment for us at the company. We were only eight people at the time, but we felt, "Hey, would people be training these very bespoke sentiment classifier models anymore that were very, very custom models? Or would they just ask GPT-N, is this a positive or a negative sentiment?" Probably it's going to be the latter, right? And in a world in which everyone was going to run generative AI models, why would an infrastructure company be a differentiator? Because everyone is going to run the same kind of infrastructure down the line. (00:06:06): So instead what we decided to do was we believe generative AI was almost going to be like the next internet. And in that case, what we should go out and do is build the next great apps like Google, like Amazon. And we vertically integrated and actually took our infrastructure, our inference infrastructure to go out and build Codeium at the time. And at that time, we were early adopters of GitHub Copilot and we thought the coding space was going to get tremendously disrupted in the next coming years. So we actually took our infrastructure, we ran our own models in massive scale. We even trained our own models. (00:06:35): In the very beginning it was very, very simple. It was purely an autocomplete model, which basically means that as the user was typing, we'd complete the next one or two or three or four lines of code. But we provided the product entirely for free in all the IDEs that developers coded. That meant to VSCode, JetBrains, Eclipse, Visual Studio, Vim, Emacs. And the reason why we were able to build it for free was because of our infrastructure background. We were able to optimize these workloads a ton. (00:07:04): I guess very quickly after that, some large businesses also wanted to work with us. And we built out this enterprise motion to work with these large companies like Dell, JPMorgan Chase. And for them the bigger thing wasn't just, "Hey, could we autocomplete code or could we chat with the code base?" It was, "Could you offer us a secure offering that was also personalized to all the private data inside the company?" So we took our infrastructure and made it so that we invested a ton in making sure that we deeply understood these large companies code bases. And that's what we were working on until six months ago. (00:07:33): It's not that we've stopped working on that, but basically what we realized six months ago was we were getting limited by the IDEs that we were already working in. So VSCode, which is a very popular IDE, had a ceiling for the AI capabilities, we could showcase our users. And because of that, we decided to go out and fork VSCode and build our own IDE with some of these new agentic capabilities. And over time in the last couple of years, the model capabilities have also been growing exponentially year over year. And that's sort of where we are right now. I skipped a lot of pieces there, but that's what we're landed.
turns.zh:
是的。这家公司实际上是在大约四年前创立的。如你所知，四年前人工智能编程还不是一个热门领域。ChatGPT那时也尚未问世。当时我们最初致力于开发GPU虚拟化和编译器软件。在此之前，我曾在自动驾驶领域工作。我从中学就相识的联合创始人当时在Meta公司从事AR/VR技术研发。我们坚信深度学习将渗透到众多行业，而不只是局限于自动驾驶领域。比如金融服务、国防、医疗保健等行业。这些深度学习应用本质上很难开发，因此我们致力于让用户无需依赖GPU就能高效运行这些复杂应用，同时为用户处理在GPU上运行工作负载的复杂任务。我们对这些工作负载进行了大量优化。  

2022年年中，我们的营收达到数百万美元，管理着超过1万台GPU服务器，当时团队仅有8人。那时我们实现了自由现金流为正。但当生成式模型开始变得极其强大时，我们意识到自己之前构建的许多应用已失去价值。这对公司来说是一个非常艰难的时刻。当时我们只有8名员工，却不得不面对这样的疑问：人们还会继续训练那些高度定制的情感分类模型吗？还是会直接询问GPT-N某段文本是积极还是消极情绪？答案显然是后者。在一个所有人都将运行生成式AI模型的世界里，基础设施公司如何脱颖而出？因为未来所有人都将采用相同的基础设施。  

因此，我们决定将生成式AI视为下一个互联网级别的技术变革。基于此，我们应该像谷歌、亚马逊等巨头那样，垂直整合基础设施，打造自己的应用。当时我们率先采用GitHub Copilot技术，认为编程领域将在未来几年迎来巨大变革。因此，我们将基础设施用于大规模模型训练和应用开发。  

最初的版本非常简单，是纯自动补全模型，即在用户输入代码时，实时补全下一行或多行。我们免费将这款产品集成到所有主流IDE中，包括VS Code、JetBrains、Eclipse、Visual Studio、Vim和Emacs。得益于我们的基础设施技术背景，我们成功优化了这些工作负载。  

很快，一些大型企业也希望与我们合作。我们为戴尔、摩根大通等企业开发了企业级解决方案。他们关心的不再是基础设施功能，而是如何安全、个性化地处理公司内部的私有数据。因此，我们投入大量精力深入理解这些大型企业的代码库，这项工作一直持续到六个月前。
倒不是说我们已经停止了相关工作，但六个月前我们意识到，现有的集成开发环境（IDE）限制了我们的发展潜力。比如说，非常流行的VS Code，其AI功能存在上限，无法完全满足用户的展示需求。因此，我们决定另辟蹊径，基于VS Code进行深度定制，开发出具备全新智能交互能力的自有IDE。过去几年间，模型处理能力也呈指数级增长。这就是我们当前的研发方向。虽然过程中省略了许多细节，但这就是我们最终的成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many interesting threads there. One is just, there's always this question of just where value will accrue in AI. And it's so interesting, you guys started almost at the bottom layer of infrastructure GPUs and then you went to what people call a GPT wrapper, not actually. So I guess any just lessons there, just thoughts on just where you think value will end up in this world of AI and the stack of AI tools?
turns.zh: 上面有好多有趣的讨论。其中一个问题是，AI领域的价值到底会体现在哪里。这非常有趣，你们最初几乎是从底层基础设施——GPU入手，然后转向了所谓的GPT封装层，但实际上并非如此。那么，关于AI世界的价值链，你们有没有什么深刻的见解，或者对于未来发展方向的思考？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Maybe I can start by just saying one thing about startups that I think are really true, it's very unlikely the first thing that you believe you should go work on is going to be the right thing, which is a very hard thing to kind of wrangle with being a startup founder, right? You need to kind of be irrationally optimistic that what you're going to do is going to be differentially important. Because otherwise, why would you go out and do what you're doing? And if it's obvious, then a bigger company would've already done it, right? (00:08:56): But then you also need to be really, really realistic because most ideas that are, I guess, non-conventional are usually bad ideas, right? So it's this weird tightrope you need to kind of balance on top of where you're pushing for a future that you believe is true, but all the while you're getting new information. You need to kill the beliefs that you had. And if I were to start with the infrastructure piece, we first went in with the assumption that model architectures were going to be really, really heterogeneous. (00:09:27): Working from an autonomous vehicle background, there were many different types of model architectures out there. There were convolutional neural networks, graph neural networks, recurrent neural networks, LSTMs, sort of lighter neural nets with frustrum point networks. And there were maybe tens of architectures we were dealing with. And at that point we were like, the complexity of this is so high that it's very clear if someone offloaded the complexity, there would be a lot of value. (00:09:50): Fast-forward to the middle of 2023, everything looks like it's going to be a transformer. So now our hypotheses are just wrong. So at this point then, most of the value is probably not going to accrue at purely the, at least this is our belief, at the infrastructure layer. It's going to accrue somewhere else. Where is the layer that you can actually differentiate on? And we believe the application layer is a very, very deep layer to go out and differentiate on, right? What are the number of ways we can build better user experiences and better workflows for developers? We think there's effectively no ceiling on that, on how much better we can make the lives of developers basically.
turns.zh:
或许我可以先谈谈我认为创业公司常遇到的一个难题：你最初认为应该投入精力开发的产品，很可能并非正确的方向。这对创业者来说确实是个挑战，因为你必须要有非理性乐观的信念，坚信自己做的事会产生独特的价值。否则，为什么还要去尝试呢？毕竟，如果一个方向显而易见，大公司早就布局了。（00:08:56）但同时你又必须保持清醒的现实感——那些看似非传统的想法往往行不通。这就好比走钢丝：一方面要坚信自己所追求的未来，另一方面又要不断获取新信息，修正错误的假设。

以基础设施为例，我们最初的假设是模型架构会极度多样化。（00:09:27）从自动驾驶领域切入时，市面上存在多种模型架构：卷积神经网络、图神经网络、循环神经网络、长短期记忆网络，还有轻量化的点云网络等，总计约十几种。当时我们认为，这些复杂性太高，若能将其抽象化必然能创造巨大价值。

但到了2023年年中，所有人都追捧Transformer模型。这意味着我们的假设完全错误。如今，价值可能不再停留在基础设施层面——至少我们认为如此。真正的价值创造点在哪里？我们认为应用层是值得深耕的领域：如何提升用户体验，优化开发者工作流？这方面的可能性几乎是无限的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You touched on the second thread that I thought was really interesting here, is just how you guys pivoted from ideas that were working. You were making money, people loved it. You said you had millions of dollars of ARR revenue. And then you're just like, "No, we're going to completely change the business." (00:10:36): So the question there is, just like, what have you learned about knowing what to follow? And one thing I heard there that was really interesting is just once your assumptions change about that you built your idea on, it's time to think this idea and maybe try something else.
turns.zh: 你提到的第二个话题也很有趣，就是你们如何从成功的业务中转型。你们当时盈利了，用户反馈不错，甚至实现了数百万美元的ARR收入。可你们却突然决定彻底改变业务模式。（00:10:36）这里我想问的是，你们在判断何时该坚持何时该转型的过程中，有哪些经验值得借鉴？比如，当你对原有假设产生质疑时，就该重新评估整个方向，尝试新的可能性。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: I think the way we sort of think about this is even when we're working right now, we just accept that we're going to get a lot of things wrong. We're just going to get a lot of things wrong. Obviously that's a very big moment because that was a bet the company moment in the sense that we basically said, told our investors, "Hey, we're making money on this." We had already raised 28 million of capital and we were just like, "Hey, we're just going to pivot entirely from this." And we did that overnight. This wasn't this thing where we just said, "Hey, maybe a quarter, one or two quarters." Because one of the things we knew that's very important for startups is focus. (00:11:20): If you're trying to do another thing that you think is big and you're focused on something that you don't believe is valuable, you're guaranteed going to fail at the thing you think is going to be big. So that's a very obvious thing there. But I think once you go in with the assumption that a lot of your hypotheses are going to be wrong, but you will do the most concentrated work possible to go out and validate these hypotheses and you won't be in love with your ideas. (00:11:41): I think ideas, it's awesome when you have a great idea, but you should never be too in love with your ideas. And you have an organization that is very truth-seeking. I think a lot of people at the company have had their ideas tested over and over again. Even just building Windsurf. That is not a complete company pivot, but that's a big decision that we made at the company. You kind of need to make some bets. And sometimes you're wrong and sometimes you're right. But if you have an organization that comes out and you feel like morale is not going to be low if you made the wrong decision, that's the best, right? That means you have optionality for the rest of time. (00:12:14): And Lenny, one thing that I try to tell the company about this is, this year the total amount of engineering output we'll have is much larger than the engineering output we've had since the beginning of the company's creation 'till now. So that almost means every year is a new lease on life for us, right? It's almost a new way for us to test out an entirely new set of hypotheses. And maybe we were wrong about our original hypotheses in the first place. What makes us more smart than everyone else to be right more times than that?
turns.zh: 我觉得我们看待这件事的方式是，即便我们现在正在工作，我们也承认自己会犯很多错误。我们注定会犯很多错误。显然，这是一个重大时刻，因为这是一次公司层面的赌注——我们基本上对投资者说：“嘿，我们能从中盈利。”当时我们已经筹集了2800万美元资金，却突然决定彻底转型。这一切都是一夜之间完成的。我们没有说"或许再等一两个季度"。因为我们深知，专注对初创公司至关重要。如果你试图做另一件自以为重大的事情，却又专注于自己认为毫无价值的东西，那么注定会在你认为会成功的事情上失败。这很明显。但我认为，一旦你带着"许多假设都会出错"的假设去行动，你就会尽可能专注地验证这些假设，同时不执着于自己的想法。（00:11:20）：我觉得有好点子当然很棒，但你永远不该过度沉溺于自己的想法。我们的公司是一个非常追求真理的组织。公司里的很多人都经历了无数次对自己想法的验证。就拿Windsurf项目来说，这虽然不是彻底的业务转型，但也是我们公司做出的重大决策。你必须做出一些赌注。有时你会错，有时又会对。但如果你有一个愿意承担错误后果的组织，那么即使做错了决定，士气也不会低落，这才是最棒的。这意味着你接下来还有选择的余地。（00:12:14）：Lenny，我想对公司说的是：今年我们的工程产出总量将远超公司创立至今的总和。这几乎意味着每年对我们来说都是新的机遇，对吧？这也是我们测试全新假设的新方式。说不定我们最初的假设就是错误的。那我们凭什么比其他人更聪明，能更频繁地做出正确判断呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so empowering. It makes me think about... Uri Levine was on the podcast, co-founder of Waze, and he has this phrase that he wears on his shirt. His book is called this Fall in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution. And that feels like that's exactly what you're describing. (00:12:59): Okay, so let's talk about Windsurf. What's the simplest way for people to understand what is Windsurf?
turns.zh: 这真是太振奋人心了。这让我想到……Waze的联合创始人乌里·莱文（Uri Levine）曾参加播客节目，他衬衫上写着这句话：爱上问题，而非解决方案。这感觉正是你所描述的。（00:12:59）：好，那我们来谈谈Windsurf吧。怎样才能让人们最简单地理解Windsurf是什么？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah. So Windsurf is an IDE, right? It's an application to go out and build software and build applications. The crazy thing is a lot of people who use the product don't even probably know what an IDE is, which is crazy. And we'll get into that in a second. (00:13:22): But why did we go out and build Windsurf and what is Windsurf maybe? Why couldn't we have just done this on top of conventional IDEs like Visual Studio Code? So maybe just to get into this a little bit, as we saw that AI was getting more and more powerful, the way people go out and build technology, we thought the interface for that was going to change remarkably. It was not going to be a conventional pure text editor where the user is writing a handful of lines of code or most of the code and the IDE provides maybe some basic feedback on what the user is doing right or wrong. And the basic feedback could be, "Hey, there's a bug in your software or compiler error in your software." It could do much more, right? It could actually go out and modify large chunks of code. (00:14:04): One of the key pieces that we recognized was, with this new paradigm with AI, AI was probably going to write well over 90% of the software, in which case the role of a developer and what they're doing in the IDE is maybe reviewing code. Maybe it's actually a little bit different than what it is in the past. And we'll see this very soon with Windsurf. Maybe when you're using the product, actually a good chunk of the user's time is that you're reviewing what the AI is outputting. So we needed to build custom-review flows into the IDE to actually make it so that it was easier to actually go out and do that, right? Because the developer is not spending all their time writing code. (00:14:38): And this is the fundamental premise on why we built the product. We thought we were going to get limited a ton if we had very, very basic UI out there. And I'll give you even a simple example here. We have this auto-complete product that completes a handful of lines of code. Now we've actually launched this offering called Windsurf Tab that basically shows you refactors as well. And these refactors are almost inline refactors. And we were able to build a custom UI for that in Windsurf. (00:15:03): But in VSCode, because of the access to the APIs, we needed to dynamically generate images right alongside the user's cursor because we just didn't have access to the capabilities to showcase and edit properly. And what we realized is immediately by porting over to Windsurf, our acceptance rate tripled. Same ML models, it just tripled. So what that, I guess, gave us confidence in is yeah, you could argue technology is very important. And I think technology is very important. But if our users are getting very little value from the technology we're sort of building, you need to really clarify, "Maybe we do need to build a new surface and interface." And that's what Windsurf is.
turns.zh: 是的。Windsurf是一款集成开发环境（IDE），对吧？它是一款用于开发软件和应用程序的工具。最令人惊讶的是，许多使用该产品的人可能甚至不知道IDE是什么，这太不可思议了。我们稍后会详细探讨这一点。  (00:13:22)：但为什么我们要开发Windsurf呢？Windsurf到底是什么？我们为什么不能直接在传统的IDE（比如Visual Studio Code）之上构建它呢？那么，让我们稍微深入探讨一下。随着AI技术越来越强大，人们开发技术的方式也在发生变化。我们认为界面设计将发生重大变革。传统的纯文本编辑器已经无法满足需求——用户通常只需编写几行代码或大部分代码，而IDE则提供一些基本的反馈，比如“你的代码有错误”或者“编译器报错”。但AI技术可以做得更多：它可以直接修改大段代码。  (00:14:04)：我们意识到，随着AI技术的发展，AI可能将编写90%以上的软件代码。在这种情况下，开发者的角色可能转变为代码审查。这与过去的情况有所不同。我们很快就会在Windsurf中看到这一点。当用户使用该产品时，他们的大部分时间可能都在审查AI输出的代码。因此，我们需要在IDE中构建定制的代码审查流程，使这一过程更加便捷。毕竟，开发者不能把所有时间都花在编写代码上。  (00:14:38)：这就是我们开发这款产品的根本原因。如果我们使用非常基础的UI，用户接受度会大打折扣。我举个简单的例子：我们有自动补全代码的功能。现在我们推出了Windsurf Tab，它可以实时显示重构建议。这些重构建议几乎是内联式的。我们能够在Windsurf中为此构建定制的UI。   (00:15:03)：但在VSCode中，由于缺乏API访问权限，我们需要动态生成图片并将其显示在用户光标旁边，因为我们无法正确展示和编辑这些内容。我们发现，一旦迁移到Windsurf，用户接受度就翻了三倍。使用相同的ML模型，效果却提升了三倍。这让我们相信，技术固然重要，但如果用户从我们开发的技术中获得的价值微乎其微，那么就必须重新审视：或许我们确实需要打造全新的界面和交互体验。这就是Windsurf的意义所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the big bet you took there just to make this super clear, is you were initially working within existing IDEs that everyone was familiar with. And then it was like, "This isn't going to get us where we need to go. We're going to try to convince people to switch to something completely new because it's going to be so much better. It's our own IDE." (00:15:56): I think maybe people may not recognize just how risky that is, convincing engineers to use something completely new. That's a huge deal.
turns.zh: 所以说，你当时做出的重大赌注（说得再直白一点）就是，你们最初是在现有的、大家都熟悉的IDE中工作。但后来发现，“这条路走不通。我们要说服人们转向全新的东西，因为它会好得多。这是我们自己的IDE。”  (00:15:56)：我觉得人们可能没有意识到，说服工程师使用全新的东西有多么冒险。这可是件大事。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah, no, of course. And one of the key pieces, maybe Lenny, that would be important to share is a lot of our developers do use Visual Studio Code. But there are lots of people that write in languages like Java, sort of C++ and so on and so forth, and they might use the JetBrains family of IDEs that like IntelliJ. And for us, we are actually still committed to building on those platforms, right? We just felt though that one of the dominant IDEs, which was Visual Studio Code, was limiting the sort of user interface that we could give to our actual customers.
turns.zh: 是的，没错，当然了。其中一个关键点——或许是莱尼（Lenny）——值得分享的是，我们许多开发者确实在使用Visual Studio Code。但也有很多人用Java、C++等语言编程，他们可能使用JetBrains旗下的IntelliJ等集成开发环境（IDE）。对我们而言，我们实际上仍致力于在这些平台上进行开发，对吧？不过我们发现，主流的IDE Visual Studio Code限制了我们能为实际客户提供的用户界面体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the current state of traction for Windsurf? You hear all these crazy numbers about all the competitors in your space. What can you share there for folks just to know?
turns.zh: Windsurf目前的吸引力如何？你听说过许多竞争对手的疯狂数据。能否为大家分享一下？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah, so maybe a handful. We launched the product a bit over four months ago. And in that period of time, over a million developers have tried the product. And obviously we have many hundreds of thousands of monthly active users right now.
turns.zh: 是的，大概有几百个吧。我们四个月前刚推出这款产品。在此期间，已有超过一百万名开发者试用了这款产品。目前我们每月活跃用户数量显然已达数十万。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how these days like, "oh, a million. Oh, no big deal." It's just the numbers are absurd these days. We're just getting used to just 100 million ARR here, million users in four months there. It's just like, "Oh, of course. How could you not have that?" But that's absurd. It's just like an insane time right now. (00:17:12): You touched on something that I wanted to get to later, but I may as well bring it up now, the question of just how engineering will change in the future. You throw out the stat that 90% of code is going to be written by AI in the future. Dario from Anthropic recently said the same thing. You guys have a really interesting glimpse into just how things will look in the future. (00:17:31): So I guess the question is just, how do you think coding specifically will look in the next few years, how different will it be from today?
turns.zh: 我很惊讶如今人们会说“哦，一百万？没什么大不了的。”如今的数字简直令人难以置信。我们刚习惯了ARR达到1亿，四个月内用户破百万。大家都觉得“哦，当然啊，不这样怎么行？”但这实在太夸张了。现在这个时代真是疯狂。（00:17:12）：你提到了我接下来想问的问题，但不妨现在就说出来，就是未来工程领域将如何变化。你提到未来90%的代码将由AI编写。Anthropic的达里奥（Dario）最近也说了同样的话。你们对未来趋势的洞察真的很深刻。（00:17:31）：所以我想问的是，未来几年编程会发生怎样的变化？与现在相比会有多大的不同？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: I think when we think about what is an engineer actually doing, it probably falls into three buckets, right? What should I solve for? How should I solve it? And then solving it. I guess everyone who's working in this space is probably increasingly convinced that solving it, which is just the pure, "I know how I'm going to do it" and just going and doing it. AI is going to handle vast majority, if not all of it. In fact, it probably actually, with some of the work that we've done in terms of deeply understanding code bases, how should I solve it is also going to get closer and closer to getting done. If you deeply understand the environment inside an organization, if you deeply understand the code base, how you should solve it, given best practices when the company also gets solved. (00:18:19): So I think what engineering kind of goes to is actually what you wanted engineers to do in the first place, which is, what are the most important business problems that we do need to solve? What are the most important capabilities that we need our application, our product to have? And actually going and prioritizing those and actually going and making the right technical decisions to go out and doing it. And I think that's where engineering is probably heading towards. (00:18:40): Now, does that mean that no one needs a CS degree? I think that's maybe a little bit overplayed a little bit just because maybe here's my argument for that. A lot of developers nowadays that build full stack applications, at least until a handful of years ago, they probably went to college and took an operating system course. And in theory, they're not really playing around with the operating system, like the kernel scheduler very frequently. But do those principles help them in understanding why their applications are slow? Do they help them in understanding why some design decisions are better than the other? Yeah, that makes them a much better engineer than another engineer. And I think that idea and the understanding of what's going on at the bottom will make a good engineer even better. But also at the same time, it empowers a bunch of people that never understood all of those things, how to actually build as well, which is another remarkable sort of thing that fell out through this whole process.
turns.zh:
我认为，当我们思考工程师实际在做什么时，大概可以分为三个方面：首先，要解决什么问题？其次，如何解决问题？最后，如何将解决方案付诸实践。我猜在这个领域工作的每个人都越来越坚信，解决问题——即明确解决方案的思路并付诸实施——这部分工作将主要由人工智能来完成。事实上，通过我们在深入理解代码库方面所做的工作，“如何解决问题”这部分也将变得越来越容易实现。若你深入了解一个组织的环境，深入理解代码库，掌握最佳实践，那么解决问题的思路也将变得更加清晰。（00:18:19）所以我认为工程师的工作本质上还是回归到最初的使命，即找出我们需要解决的最重要的业务问题，以及我们的应用或产品需要具备的最重要的功能。然后，优先处理这些问题，做出正确的技术决策并付诸实践。我认为这才是工程师们正在朝着的方向发展。

（00:18:40）但这是否意味着不需要计算机科学学位呢？我认为这或许有些夸大其词了。举个例子：如今许多开发全栈应用的开发者（至少在过去几年里）可能上过大学，学习过操作系统课程。虽然他们实际上并不频繁地研究操作系统内核调度器之类的内容，但这些原理能帮助他们理解应用为何运行缓慢，能帮助他们判断某种设计决策是否更优。这些知识能让他们成为比其他工程师更出色的开发者。我认为对底层原理的理解能让优秀的工程师更上一层楼，同时也让许多原本对这些技术一知半解的人也能成功开发应用，这真是整个过程带来的惊喜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if you have kids, but just say you had kids or you had niece or nephew going into college, let's say, would you suggest they do do computer science or would you suggest you're not going to have a good time if that's the career you choose right now?
turns.zh: 不知道你是否有孩子，但假设你有孩子，或者有侄子侄女即将上大学，你会建议他们选择计算机科学专业吗？还是会告诉他们，如果选择这个职业，现在可能还不会有太好的体验？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah. Maybe I think back a little bit. So I went to MIT. A lot of us at the company went to MIT together on the engineering team. I think when I think about what we learned the most for engineering or computer science, it was not exactly like how do you write code. That is almost a given that you can write code after going to college. It's more like the principles of how you think about a problem and how you break it down and how you solve it in an interesting way. (00:20:15): So an example of a class that I really enjoyed was our distributed systems class. And there, you're kind of reading through literature and understanding how some design decisions were kind of made. And I think it's more like a problem solving kind of course and a major. It's a major of how you solve problems given some constraints of how computers today function, right? Like, here's the speed at which memory sort of operates. Here's the speed at which... Here's how much computation you can do in one cycle or one second. And based on that, you can make some trade-offs and solve a problem. (00:20:45): So I don't know if I would say that you shouldn't go get a computer science degree. I think computer science is almost synonymous with problem solving. In that case, I think it's pretty valuable. Is everything you learn in your computer science degree useful? I'd say a lot of things that I learned in my computer science degree are not useful. I'll give you an example. I took a parallel computing class in Julia. I don't think Julia is a very popular programming language anymore. Am I very sad that I took the class? No. The principles of parallel computing are still very useful, I would say, today.
turns.zh: 是的。或许我会回想一下过去。当时我上了麻省理工学院（MIT）。在公司里，很多工程团队成员都曾就读于麻省理工。我觉得回想起在工程或计算机科学方面学到的最重要东西，并不完全是如何编写代码——毕竟上了大学后会编写代码几乎是理所当然的。更重要的是如何思考问题，如何分解问题，以及如何以巧妙的方式解决问题。（00:20:15）举个我特别喜欢的课程例子——分布式系统课。在那门课上，我们会通读相关文献，理解某些设计决策是如何做出的。我认为这门课本质上是关于解决问题的，也是一门重要的专业。它教会你如何在当今计算机运作的限制条件下解决问题，比如内存运行速度、每秒可处理的计算量等。基于这些限制，你可以做出权衡取舍，最终解决问题。（00:20:45）所以我不认为应该劝人别去读计算机科学学位。我觉得计算机科学几乎等同于解决问题的能力。在这种情况下，它确实很有价值。计算机科学学位里学的所有内容都有用吗？我得说，我学到的很多东西都没用。我举个例子。我上过Julia语言的并行计算课，但Julia现在已经不是很流行的编程语言了。我会因此感到遗憾吗？不。并行计算的原理在今天仍然非常有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing is, skills that you still want to build, whether it's computer science or maybe some version of computer science, is kind of building the mental model of how computers and systems work.
turns.zh: 所以我的理解是，无论是计算机科学还是类似的专业，人们真正想培养的技能都是建立计算机和系统运作的思维模型。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Parallel processing, memory, hard drives, internet, things like that. And then there's just problem solving skills, being able to solve interesting problems. Is there any other skills you think people should be investing more in with the rise of AI building more and more of our products?
turns.zh: 并行处理、内存、硬盘、互联网之类的。还有解决问题的能力，能够解决有趣的问题。随着人工智能越来越多地参与产品开发，你认为人们还应该在哪些技能上投入更多精力？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: I think one of the things that's maybe a little bit undervalued is this kind of agency piece. And I think about this a lot, which is, you have a lot of people that could go through college and go through school and they're basically told exactly what to do on a P-set. They're given these very, very, I would say, well-defined paths that they need to take. I think maybe in society and just school, we don't prioritize how do you make sure you get people with real agency that want to build something, right? Their goal is not just to maybe graduate from college and then get a job at a big tech company where they're told exactly what to do or where to put the pixel for this one website. I think that's maybe a skill set that is undervalued just right now, probably in the last maybe 10 years or so. And I think that's going to be really, really important. (00:22:27): For a startup, obviously these are skills that we just look for. We look for people that are really high agency because we just recognize that by default, if we don't innovate and do crazy things, we're going to die. The company is just going to die. So we just look for this, right? But I would say for most software engineering jobs, that's probably not the case. Just think about big company X and what they're hiring for on the average software engineering interview. It probably doesn't look like that.
turns.zh:
我觉得有一点可能被低估了，那就是这种自主决策的能力。我对此思考良多——很多学生在大学或学校里学习时，基本上都是被告知该如何完成作业。他们被赋予了非常明确的学习路径，必须严格遵循。我认为，在社会和教育体系中，我们没有充分重视如何培养那些真正有自主决策能力、渴望有所建树的人才。他们不只是为了从大学毕业，然后在大科技公司找份工作，被告知如何操作某个网站的像素点。我觉得这种技能组合在当下被严重低估了，可能在过去十年左右的时间里都是如此。但未来它将变得至关重要。

（00:22:27）对于初创公司来说，显然我们特别看重这种自主决策能力。因为我们深知，如果不创新、不尝试突破常规，公司注定会消亡。所以我们必须具备这种能力。但对于大多数软件工程岗位来说，情况可能并非如此。想想某个大型科技公司，他们在平均水平的软件工程面试中招聘人才时，通常不会看重这种能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how you phrased that. If we don't do crazy things and innovate, we're going to die. That would be a great title for this podcast episode. And I think, I know, it's 100% true. There's just a lot of crazy things happening and a lot of innovation happening. And if you can't keep up, you'll die. (00:23:07): So let's talk about hiring. You have a really interesting approach to hiring. There's a few questions I have here. One is just how do you... I know you try to stay really lean. That's a common theme across all the AI startups these days. How do you know when it's time to hire someone?
turns.zh:
我很欣赏你这样表达：如果我们不创新、不尝试疯狂的举措，我们就会被淘汰。这简直可以作为本期播客的绝佳标题。我深信这是千真万确的。当下确实有很多疯狂的尝试和创新。如果你跟不上时代，就会被淘汰。

（00:23:07）接下来聊聊招聘问题。你的招聘策略很独特。我有几个问题想问。首先，你如何……我知道你致力于保持团队精简。这是当下所有AI初创公司的共同特点。那你如何判断何时该招聘新人呢？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: I love the idea of being a lean company, but I don't idolize it in the way that, "Hey, it is a dream to be a 10% or 20% company that's making 50, 100, 200 million in revenue." That's not, I think, what we idolize inside the company. (00:23:36): I think what we idolize is, be the smallest company we can be to satisfy our ambitions. That's what the goal is. And maybe, Lenny, the way I would sort of put that out there is, if I told you, "Hey, I'm going to build an autonomous vehicle," and I said our team is 10 people, you should rightfully say, "Hey Varun, you're not serious. And you'd be right. I'm not serious at that point. So I think the answer is, what is the minimum number of people to go out and build the crazy ambition project that you have? (00:24:04): And I think the project we are trying to go out and do, which is completely transform the way software gets built, we've mentioned this [inaudible 00:24:11] the company, our goal is to reduce the time it takes to build apps and technology by 99%, right? It is a tremendously sort of ambitious goal. And it's not possible for us to be a 10, 20, 30, 40 person engineering team in the long term and actually satisfy that goal. We think there's a very, very high ceiling. So that's maybe the first key piece there. It's like, if we can crack actually being a fairly sizable company but still operate as if we're a startup, that's the dream. That's the dream. (00:24:40): In terms of hiring philosophy, the way we sort of think about things is, we only hire for a role if we're actually underwater for that function. So let's say we're going out and building inference technology. Unless we're underwater there, we will not go out and hire someone to go out and work for that. And the reason for that is, I actually think this is a feature. When you hire for a role and you already have enough people there, you get a lot of weird politics that ultimately ends up happening. And it's not because people are bad people. I think most people are really well-intentioned. But what happens when you have people that join a company and in reality you didn't really need them? They will go out and manufacture some other thing that they should go work on. They will go out and figure out something else to work on. And realistically, it's not that important, but they will go out and try to convince the rest of the organization that it is important. (00:25:30): I just think as a startup, we don't have the bandwidth to go out and deal with that, right? For me, I would like to see everyone just almost be raising their hands up being like, "I'm dying. We need one more person." And that's when we go out and hire someone. And one of the analogies I like to give is, I want the company to almost be this dehydrated entity and every hire is like a little bit of water. And we only go back and hire someone when we're back to being dehydrated.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏精益管理的理念，但我不把它奉为神话。比如，“成为营收5千万、1亿、2亿的10%或20%规模的公司”，这种想法在我看来并非我们公司所推崇的。（00:23:36）我认为我们真正推崇的，是以最小规模的团队来实现我们的宏伟抱负。这才是目标所在。或许，伦尼，我可以这样说——如果你对我说：“嘿，我要开发自动驾驶汽车”，然后告诉我团队只有10个人，你完全有理由说：“嘿，瓦伦，你不是认真的吧。”你说得没错。当时我确实不认真。但我认为问题的关键在于：要想实现开发疯狂项目的目标，所需的最小团队规模是多少？（00:24:04）就拿我们正致力于彻底变革软件开发方式的项目来说吧，我们曾提到（此处音频不清晰）公司的目标是将应用和技术开发时间缩短99%。这是一个极具挑战性的目标。但从长远来看，我们不可能维持一个由10人、20人、30人、40人组成的工程团队来达成这个目标。我们相信这是一个极高的天花板。所以这或许是首要关键点。关键在于：如果我们能在保持创业精神的同时，成为规模可观的公司，那才是梦想。（00:24:40）在招聘理念上，我们的思路是，只有当某个职位存在实际空缺时，才会去招聘。比如说，我们要开发推理技术。除非这个职位存在空缺，否则我们不会去招聘相关人才。原因在于，我认为这本身就是一个优点。当你为一个已有充足人力的职位招聘时，总会引发各种复杂的权力斗争。这并非因为人们品行不端——我相信大多数人都是善意的。但当新加入的员工实际上并非团队所需时，他们会另辟蹊径，试图说服其他人这个职位至关重要。（00:25:30）我认为作为一家初创公司，我们根本没有精力去应对这些复杂局面。对我而言，我希望看到每个人都迫不及待地举手说：“我们快撑不住了，我们还需要一个人。”然后我们才会去招聘。我常用的一个比喻是，我希望公司像一个干涸的实体，而每次招聘都是一滴水。当我们重新陷入资源不足的境地时，才会去招聘新人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this metaphor so much. And it sounds painful. It sounds painful that you need to be underwater and raising your hand, "I'm about to die and dehydrated." But I also know that it's a really exciting way to work. It sounds hard, but if you're in it, it's just like... I guess talk about just that side of it because I think it could sound like, "This is terrible. I don't want to work this way."
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个比喻了。听起来很痛苦。被迫举手说：“我快撑不住了，我们急需一个人。”听起来很痛苦。但我也知道这是一种令人兴奋的工作方式。听起来很艰难，但如果你身处其中，就会觉得……我觉得就谈谈这方面吧，因为我觉得听起来可能像是“这太糟糕了，我不想这样工作”。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: You know what I actually think, Lenny? It's really good for a handful of reasons, which is that a lot of the... We respect and trust the people that work at the company. So this forces ruthless prioritization. You have a team that's going out and doing something. They will never ask to work on something that's not important. In fact, if there are two things that they're working on, they're just going to just tell me, "Hey, there are two things on my plate. I just don't have the ability to do two. I can only do one." And they will pick the one that's most important. (00:26:45): And this actually goes back to one thing that I think is true about startups and just companies in general. You don't win by doing 10 things well. You win by doing one thing really well and maybe you fail nine things. This is the thing that I've told the company, "This is very different than school," right? In school you optimize for your total GPA. But for companies, I just need to get an A+ on the one class that matters. And then I can get an F in all the other classes. And an F in all the other classes doesn't mean just doing illegal things. That basically means you just deprioritize things that don't matter. That actually forces this organizational prioritization that is just really, really good. (00:27:22): And Douglas and I, Douglas being my co-founder, we can tell the company, "These are the two things that are the most important." But if we go out and tell these are the two things that are the most important to the company and then we put the company has 20% more people than necessary, what's going to ultimately happen? It's almost a forcing function for ruthless prioritization to have fewer people or people that are just underwater internally at the company.
turns.zh: 伦尼，你知道我怎么想的吗？这其实很棒，原因有几个。首先，我们尊重并信任公司里的每一位员工。这就迫使我们必须无情地设定优先级。团队出去做事时，他们绝不会主动要求去做不重要的事。事实上，如果他们同时负责两件事，他们会直接告诉我：“嘿，我手头有两件事要做，但我没能力同时做两件事，只能做一件事。”然后他们会选择最重要的那件事。（00:26:45）这其实让我想到了一点——无论是初创公司还是一般公司，成功的关键不在于把十件事都做得好，而是把一件事做到极致，可能其他九件事做得不尽如人意。这就是我跟公司说的“这和学校很不一样”对吧？在学校里，你要优化整体GPA，但在公司里，我只需要在最重要的项目上拿A+，其他项目哪怕拿F也不意味着做错事，而是意味着你会把不重要的事放在次要位置。这实际上迫使公司形成一种非常高效的优先级管理机制。（00:27:22）道格拉斯和我——道格拉斯是我的联合创始人——可以告诉公司：“这两件事是公司最重要的。”但如果我们出去说这两件事对公司最重要，结果却招了比需要多20%的人进来，最终会怎样？少人或者内部资源不足其实就是无情设定优先级的必要条件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everyone listening that works at a big company knows exactly what you mean when you described when there's just too many people, they will all find work to do and they will all be pitching ideas. They all want to show impact, they want to do well in their performance reviews. That's just the nature of too many people at a company. And so I think this all really resonates. (00:28:04): To even getting even deeper on just what it looks like when someone's underwater to tell you it's time to hire, is it just someone coming to you, "Varun, I need someone on this team. This is just not possible"? What does that look like even more practically?
turns.zh: 在大公司工作的听众们肯定深有体会，当人手过多时，每个人都会找事做，都会不断提想法。他们都想显山露水，都想在绩效评估中表现出色。这就是大公司人手过多时的常态。所以我觉得你说的这些都非常有共鸣。（00:28:04）再深入一点，如何判断某人是否“资源不足”从而需要招聘？是不是有人直接来找你说：“瓦伦，这个团队需要人手，但现在根本不行。”具体表现是什么样的？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's basically along those lines. It's that, "Hey, there's some pressure to get something done in a short period of time." By the way, one of the things that we do believe though for software, if you want to do great things, it's not possible to just say, "Hey, I want to get it done in one month" if it is like... Because you have to think about it from this perspective. If a software project could get built in two to three weeks, what does that really mean about the true complexity and differentiation of what you built? It's probably not very high, unless you believe you are way smarter than everyone else. But I think that's hubris, right? I think we actually have a very exceptional engineering team. But also at the same time, I don't think our engineering team is so exceptional that we can do things in three weeks that the rest of the world can't do in six to nine months. That's kind of stupid to believe that. (00:28:57): So I think basically it comes down to that person coming out and being like, "Hey, look, I don't have enough time to do X." Us having a conversation to be like, "Okay, what can you do then?" And if the answer is, "I can only do less than that," then maybe we make a decision actually, "Oh wow, that's great. Maybe we actually should deprioritize Y." Because this is actually also another thing that's very hard even for people like me and my co-founder. It's that we also want to do a lot of things. There's an urge to do a lot of things. But if we are forced to make a decision constantly on like, "We cannot do X," it's very clarifying. It's very clarifying because our engineering interview process is also extremely low acceptance rate. So it's not very easy for us to very quickly spin up people and have them join the company really, really quickly either. (00:29:43): So I think it's clarifying for everyone. It's clarifying for the person that wants more people. We can just tell them, "Hey look, we don't believe you should be doing this other thing." And it's also clarifying for us because we can also get on the same page with them. And sometimes we just kind of agree, "Hey..." Our teams are very flexible that, "Hey, actually we do need to get something done." And one of the things that we've kind of tried to make sure is true on our engineering team is, people's value to the company does not have anything to do with the size of their team. There are projects inside the company, there are directly responsible individuals for these projects inside the company. And if we feel like one project is very important, then people can move from one project to the next. (00:30:21): There's no notion of someone owning people at the company. That is a very bad and gnarly idea. In fact, the person that is the most valuable at the company is the person that can do the most crazy sort of project out there with as few people as possible. And that's what you should be rewarding internally.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得基本就是这么个意思。就是，“嘿，短期内完成某件事确实有压力。”不过说到软件开发，我们确实认为，如果你想做出伟大的成果，光说 “嘿，我想在一个月内完成” 是行不通的，除非……因为你得从这个角度去考虑。如果一个软件项目能在两到三周内完成，那这真的能说明你所开发的东西的复杂性和差异化有多高吗？很可能不高——除非你觉得自己比别人聪明得多。但我觉得这太自大了。我认为我们的工程团队确实非常出色。但与此同时，我不认为我们的工程团队强大到能在三周内完成其他团队需要六到九个月才能完成的任务。这种想法太不现实了。（00:28:57）所以我觉得关键在于，当有人站出来说：“嘿，看，我没有足够的时间做 X 了。” 我们会聊聊：“好，那你能做些什么？” 如果回答是“我只能做得更少”，或许我们就会决定：“哇，太好了。或许我们应该把 Y 项目的优先级降下来。” 因为这其实也是个很难解决的问题，即使对我和我的联合创始人来说也是如此。我们也想做很多事情，有种迫切感。但如果我们被迫不断做出决定，比如 “我们做不了 X 项目” ，这其实很明智。明智之处在于我们的工程面试流程通过率极低。所以我们很难快速招来新人，让他们很快加入公司。（00:29:43）所以我觉得这对每个人都很清晰。对想招更多人的人来说我们可以直接说：“嘿，看，我们觉得你不应该做这个其他项目。” 对我们自己来说也很清晰，因为我们能和他们达成共识。有时我们会达成一致：“嘿……” 我们的团队非常灵活，如果真的有项目需要完成，我们就能动员起来。（00:30:21）公司里没有人拥有其他人的情况。这种想法非常糟糕、非常不健康。事实上，公司里最有价值的人，是能用最少的人完成最疯狂项目的人。这种人值得内部奖励。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How many people do you have at coding at this point?
turns.zh: 你们现在编码部门有多少人？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: So we have close to 160 people and the engineering team is over 50 people right now.
turns.zh: 我们现在有接近160人，工程团队有50多人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Oh, what's the other bigger functions? So [inaudible 00:30:46]-
turns.zh: 太棒了。哦，还有其他大的部门吗？比如 [听不清 00:30:46] -

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: We have go-to-market. We have a... Yeah.
turns.zh: 我们有市场推广部门。我们还有个……对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, right. Okay. I want to talk about that, the sales learning that you guys had. Okay. But let's close out this hiring conversation. So we talked about what you look for... To tell you it's the time to hire, what do you look for in the people that you interview and hire?
turns.zh: 哦，对。好的。我想谈谈你们的销售学习经历。好的。但先结束这次招聘对话吧。我们已经讨论了你们所寻找的条件……现在要说的是招聘时机，你们在面试和招聘员工时最看重什么？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: One of the key pieces that we look for, we have a very high technical bar. So assuming that they actually meet the technical bar, I think we sort of look for people that are really, really passionate about the mission of what we're actually trying to solve and people that are willing to work very hard. I think one of the things that we don't try to do is convince people, "Hey look, we are a very chill company and it's great to work here." I think, no, this is a very exciting space. It's very competitive. You should expect us to lose if the people at the company are not kind of... They're not working very hard. And I think one of the biggest dog whistles I hear is, when I ask people how hard are you willing to work, some people actually ultimately say, "Hey, I work very smart." And I basically ask them a question, "If we have many smart people at our company that also work hard, what's the differentiator going to be? Are you just going to pull them down?" (00:31:48): Because I think one of the things that's true about companies is it's like this massive group project. And I think the thing about a person that is not pulling their weight that's bad. It's not the productivity, right? At some point when the company becomes many hundreds of engineers, I'm not going to be thinking about the one engineer that's not pulling their weight. It's the team of people they work with that are almost basically saying, "Is this the bar internally at the company? Is this the expectation?" And I guess, Lenny, if I told you you have a team of five people and the four other people you're working with just don't care, how much are you going to feel like you should care?
turns.zh: 我们最看重的一点是技术门槛很高。所以假设候选人能达到技术标准，我觉得我们更关注的是那些对我们试图解决的核心使命充满热情，并且愿意付出巨大努力的人。我认为我们不会试图用一些花哨的说辞来吸引人才，比如“我们公司很轻松，工作环境很棒”。相反，我会强调这个领域竞争激烈，充满挑战。如果团队成员不全力以赴，我们注定会失败。（00:31:48）我觉得公司本质上就是一个大型团队项目。一个不尽全力的人带来的影响是致命的。关键不在于生产力——当公司发展到数百名工程师时，个人的表现对整体影响微乎其微。真正的问题在于团队成员会互相质疑：“这是公司的内部标准吗？这是大家应有的期望吗？”比如，莱尼，如果你所在的团队有五个人，其他四个人都不上心，你觉得自己该怎么做？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not too much.
turns.zh: 不会太在意。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Exactly. So for us, I think that's what we more care about. We have a culture where it's very collaborative. It's not an individual sport, but people feel like they can rely on other people to get complex sort of tasks done.
turns.zh: 没错。所以对我们来说，更看重的是团队协作文化。这不是个人英雄主义，而是每个人都能依赖他人完成复杂任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the question you asked there just basically is, how hard are you willing to work? How hard do you want to work? And I know some people, there's this whole group of folks that are just like work-life balance, "How dare you ask me to work crazy hours?" And I love just the filter upfront of, "If you work here, you will work really hard. You'll work a lot of hours. It's a crazy space to be in. And we will win by working smart and also really hard."
turns.zh: 你提到的那个问题，本质上就是“你愿意付出多大的努力？”我知道有些人总强调工作与生活的平衡，觉得“怎么能要求我们疯狂加班？”但我们从一开始就会明确：在这里工作，你必须全力以赴，投入大量时间。这是个高压环境，我们必须通过智慧和勤奋取胜。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said at some point earlier that your engineering pass rate, as you said, it was like 0.6% of candidates, something like that.
turns.zh: 你之前提到过，你们公司的工程师通过率很低，大概只有0.6%左右。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah, it's probably post or take home. It's probably that actually. So the take home itself filters probably another 10, 15X on top of that.
turns.zh: 是的，可能更像是面试后再决定录用，大概就是这样。所以最终的录用率可能还要再筛选一遍，降低10到15倍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Here's a question that I've been hearing more and more, is just, how do you do interviews these days with tools like Windsurf out there that solve all your problems?
turns.zh: 现在越来越多人问这个问题：在Windsurf等工具解决了所有招聘难题的背景下，如今的面试该怎么做？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: We are okay with people using the tools because I think one of the worst things is like, if someone comes here and doesn't like using these tools, we believe there are massive productivity improvements. We do bring people into the company on site so we can actually see how they think through problems on a whiteboard and all these other pieces. So we do want to see how they think on their feet and hopefully they're not just taking what we're saying, putting it in a voice translator and sticking it into ChatGPT and getting the answer out. (00:33:51): So there is a way to do this. My viewpoint on this is the tools are really, really important, but I do think we still look for some problem solving ability. If the only way you can solve a hard problem is put it into ChatGPT, I think that's a concern to us.
turns.zh: 我们不介意人们使用这些工具，因为我认为最糟糕的情况是，如果有人来到这里却不喜欢使用这些工具，我们相信这会极大地提升生产力。我们确实会让新员工到公司现场办公，这样我们就能亲眼看到他们如何在白板上思考问题，以及处理其他事务。因此，我们希望看到他们能够随机应变地思考问题，而不是简单地把我们说的话输入语音翻译器，再塞进ChatGPT里获取答案。（00:33:51）：当然，还是有办法做到这一点的。我对此的看法是，这些工具确实非常重要，但我们仍然会寻找解决问题的能力。若你只能通过把难题输入ChatGPT来解决问题，我认为这对我们来说是个担忧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today's episode is brought to you by Coda. I personally use Coda every single day to manage my podcast and also to manage my community.
