turns.zh: 一款不错的狗狗应用程序。其中很酷的一点是，我们不仅仅是修改代码，还能够指向不同的组件。我想我可以这么说……我可以指向不同的元素，然后说：“嘿，把背景改成……” 这设计不算太好，但我基本上可以说，如果我选中这个元素，“把这个背景改成红色”，就能直接更改并生效。（00:45:52）：产品的预览功能能在应用开发过程中展示效果，这很有帮助。现在你完全可以沉浸在应用世界里，不需要再看代码了。当然这看起来很糟糕，但如果我想的话，我还是能去改的，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is what happens when there's no more designers. Like, [inaudible 00:46:11].
turns.zh: 这就是没有设计师时会出现的情况。比如，[00:46:11听不清]。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah. When there's no more designers. Sure. Maybe the answer is like, when you ask me what should people be doing, they should study great taste. Having great taste. Because I think taste is also a very, very hard, right? (00:46:22): But maybe the other key piece, Lenny, that I wanted to showcase here is obviously you could keep going here. I could take different components and kind of change them. We have a lot of plans here that are beyond just point and click changing components. But one of the cool pieces is the AI. There's an AI review flow as well, which is kind of like what I was saying. The goal of AI has now changed a lot in that it is now modifying large chunks of code for you. And the job of a developer now is to actually review a lot of the code that the AI has generated. And granted right now during this podcast, I'm not going to review all the code that's getting generated. (00:46:57): But let's say I want to go out and modify some of this code. And this is where if you're an actual developer that actually wants to go modify, maybe I don't like my variable name being called title. I want it to be called Title String instead, like this. And if I wanted to go out and make that change and change to go out and say Title String and that's what I'm going to do, I'm just going to tell the AI to continue. (00:47:18): The cool part about this is Windsurf not only knows about what the agent has done. It also knows everything that the user has done. Our goal here is to have this almost flow-like state where everything the user has done, the AI also knows. And it is able to predict the intent. And as you can see, it said, "I noticed that the interface property title was changed to Title String." And then it now has gone out and modified all the locations within the app from title to Title String. And now it no longer says that. (00:47:45): So this is where even if I'm writing software and I want to go and make point changes, the AI can go out and quickly make these changes on the user's path. Imagine doing a refactor or a migration and you just change one part of the code. You can just tell the AI to continue the rest. And because it deeply understands the code base, it should go out and find all the corresponding places to go out and make the change. And obviously now when I reload my app, there's no bug in the app. It still loads properly. I could obviously tell it to do even cooler things like make the app retro. I don't know what that means, but I guess I could do that. And it should go out and make the change correspondingly for me. (00:48:23): But yeah, that's maybe the high level parts there where the AI is not only able to operate entirely in app space but also on the code space of the users going out and modifying code and to bridge the gap between the two. So it should add leverage not only non-developers that are just purely building apps, but also developers that are just hands-on keyboard too.
turns.zh: 是啊。当设计师都消失的时候。当然。或许答案是，当你问我人们应该做什么时，他们应该学习优秀的审美。拥有良好的审美能力。因为我认为审美能力也非常、非常难掌握，对吧？（00:46:22）不过，莱尼，我想在这里展示的另一个关键点显然是，你可以继续探索这里。我可以调整不同的组件。我们有很多计划，不只是点击鼠标更改组件。但其中很酷的一点是人工智能。这里还有人工智能审核流程，这正是我之前所说的。人工智能的目标现在已经发生了很大变化，它现在会为你修改大段代码。而开发者的任务现在是实际审查人工智能生成的大量代码。当然，在这次播客中，我不会审查所有生成的代码。（00:46:57）但假设我想出去修改一些代码。比如，我不喜欢变量名被称为title，我想把它改成Title String。然后我要去修改，我只需要告诉人工智能继续。（00:47:18）酷的地方在于，Windsurf不仅知道代理做了什么，还知道用户做了什么。我们的目标是实现一种近乎流畅的状态，用户做的所有操作，人工智能都能知晓。它能够预测用户的意图。正如你所看到的，它说"我注意到接口属性title被改成了Title String。"然后它现在已经在应用中把所有地方都改成了Title String。现在它不再提示这个了。（00:47:45）所以即使我在编写软件，想要进行点级修改，人工智能也能在用户的路径上快速进行这些修改。想象一下重构或迁移，你只改动了代码的一部分。你可以告诉人工智能继续处理剩下的部分。由于它对代码库有深刻理解，它应该能找到所有对应的地方并进行修改。显然，现在当我重新加载应用时，应用中没有任何错误。它仍然能正常加载。我当然可以让它做更酷的事情，比如把应用做成复古风格。我不知道这意味着什么，但我想我可以做到。然后它应该相应地为我进行修改。（00:48:23）不过是的，这或许就是高层次的部分，人工智能不仅能够完全在应用空间中操作，还能在用户修改代码的代码空间中操作，从而弥合两者之间的差距。因此，它不仅能为那些只是纯粹开发应用的非开发者增添助力，也能为那些亲自敲键盘的开发者带来便利。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. By the way, if you're not on YouTube, you can't see, but you can just select any element of the page and then reference that in your ask of, "Here's what I want changed." I didn't know that was a feature. And that is extremely cool. (00:48:57): So interestingly, so having just looked at Lovable and Bolt and Replit and apps like that, it's basically doing all the things those apps do. Oh, wow. There's the retro version. That's good. I like that it built on your red and made it really nice actually.
turns.zh: 太棒了。顺便说一句，如果你不在YouTube上，你看不到，但你可以选择页面的任何元素，然后在你的请求中引用它，比如"这就是我想要改动的地方。"我不知道这是一个功能。这真是太酷了。（00:48:57）所以有趣的是，我看了Lovable、Bolt、Replit和类似的应用，它们基本上都在做这些应用所做的一切。哦，哇。这是复古版本。不错。我喜欢它基于你的红色主题进行构建，实际上做得非常好。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Actually the red looks way better now.
turns.zh: 实际上现在这红色看起来好多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, a little green button. This is great. Okay.
turns.zh: 是的，一个小小的绿色按钮。这太棒了。好的。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I don't think people realize this, but apps like Windsurf, that it could actually do a lot of agentic work for you where you just tell it, "Here. I want you to do this" versus it's auto completing code for you. (00:49:25): The big difference is you need to start it with some code base so you have this kind of boilerplate React project. Is there a reason you guys aren't taking that step and just doing that automatically for you? Is it because you're targeting engineers and they don't need that or is there other reasons?
turns.zh: 所以我觉得人们可能没意识到，像Windsurf这样的应用，它实际上能为你做很多代理性工作——你只需要告诉它，“这里。我想让你做这个”，而不是让它自动帮你完成代码。（00:49:25）：最大的区别在于，你需要用一些代码库来启动它，这样你才能有那种模板化的React项目。你们为什么不采取这一步，直接自动为用户生成呢？是因为你们的目标用户是工程师，他们不需要这些功能，还是有其他原因？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Lenny, the interesting thing is the base app that you saw for this was also generated by Windsurf. The reason why we sort of didn't generate it is installing all the dependencies takes like three or four minutes. And for the demo, I didn't want to wait. But totally, actually most of the users of the product, probably zero-to-one build these apps. (00:49:57): And if I can say one interesting thing is, when we launched Windsurf, actually we tasked everyone at our company to go out and build an app with Windsurf. That included our go-to market team and our sales team. There was a crazy stat that I think people would find surprising, but we've saved over half a million dollars of SaaS products we were going to buy because our go-to-market team has now built apps instead of buying them. Our head of partnerships, instead of buying a partner portal product, has actually built its own partner portal. He had never built software in the past. We've actually come up with ways inside the company to deploy these apps easily in a secure way. And we're actually now building very, very custom software for our company to operate more efficiently, which is, I would not have expected this probably six months ago.
turns.zh: 莱尼，有趣的是你看到的这个基础应用也是由Windsurf生成的。我们没有生成它的原因是安装所有依赖项需要三到四分钟。为了演示，我不想等那么久。不过说真的，实际上大多数用户可能零到一地构建这些应用。（00:49:57）：如果我能说一件有趣的事，那就是我们推出Windsurf时，实际上让公司里的每个人都去用Windsurf构建应用。这包括我们的市场团队和销售团队。有一个令人惊讶的数据，我想大家可能会觉得很意外——我们已经节省了超过50万美元原本打算购买的SaaS产品，因为我们的市场团队现在自己构建应用而不是购买。我们的合作伙伴负责人原本打算购买合作伙伴门户产品，现在却自己构建了一个。他以前从未编写过软件。我们实际上在公司内部想出了方法，可以轻松、安全地部署这些应用。现在我们正在为公司开发非常定制化的软件，以提高运营效率。这是我六个月前根本没想到的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is incredibly interesting. You don't need to name company names, but I guess what's a space you're least bullish on that you think is going to have the most problem here with people building their own version of these sorts of products?
turns.zh: 这真是太有趣了。你不需要说出公司名称，但我想问一下，你们最不看好的领域是哪个？你认为哪个领域在人们自己开发这类产品时会遇到最大的问题？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: I think maybe my viewpoint are these very, very verticalized niche products I think are going to get... They're going to get competed down a ton. And I think sales products are an example of one of these things. And maybe this is a... I don't want to be very negative, but it's very hard inside a company like ours to task our best engineers to build a best in class sales product. There's not enough interest to do that. Or to build a best in class legal software product or finance software product. It's very, very hard for us to. And actually that's a very big moat for these companies that built these products that they were able to come out, have an opinionated stance on how to do this, hire good enough engineers to go out and build the software. Our company is unwilling to do that. So previously, we would go out and buy the technology because there would be no alternative. (00:51:48): But now one of the crazy things is that the domain specialists now have access to build the tools that they ultimately wanted, which is actually crazy. If you think about why were these software companies able to exist these vertical software companies, the reason is because they had many features. The kitchen sink of features worked for a lot of companies, but each individual company only wanted 10% of the features. But the problem is, each individual company was not capable of maintaining a piece of software or building the custom piece of software for 10% of the features, but that has now changed entirely. Now they can.
turns.zh: 我觉得可能我的观点是，这些垂直度极高的利基产品会面临激烈竞争。我认为销售类产品就是其中一个例子。我不想太悲观，但在我们这样的公司内部，要派最优秀的工程师去开发一流的销售软件实在太难了。大家对此缺乏足够的兴趣。即便开发法律软件或财务软件，也面临同样的挑战。对我们来说，这实在太难了。实际上，这正是那些成功打造此类产品的公司的巨大护城河——他们能够站稳脚跟，拥有清晰的技术路线图，招募到足够优秀的工程师去开发软件。而我们公司却不愿这样做。以前，我们只能被迫收购技术，因为别无选择。（00:51:48）但现在最疯狂的是，领域专家现在能够自主开发他们真正想要的工具，这实在太不可思议了。回想一下，为什么这些垂直软件公司能够存在？原因在于它们提供了丰富的功能。面面俱到的功能套件对许多公司有效，但每个公司只需要10%的功能。但问题是，每个公司都无法维护或为10%的功能定制软件，而现在情况完全改变了。现在他们可以做到了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. There's always been a story of like, "Why would I spend any time building my own software if I could just..." But now it's like five minutes of time.
turns.zh: 是啊，总有一种说法：“如果我能直接买现成的软件，为什么还要自己开发？”但现在只需要五分钟时间。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Five minutes and maybe even more custom to your system. How many times have you bought a software and you're almost like, "Why is there no integration to X? And I actually use X." How annoying is that? That actually makes the software less useful to you.
turns.zh: 五分钟时间，甚至可能根据你的系统进行更多定制。你有多少次购买软件后，会忍不住问：“为什么没有和X的集成？而我明明在用X啊。”这多让人心烦啊？这实际上让软件对你的实用性大打折扣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I think what's cool is when you go back, if someone zooms back to the beginning of when you started the demo, it's basically a PM talking to an engineer, "Hey, build me a Airbnb for dogs. Here's a stupid mock that I made with some boxes." That's almost like a bad PM talking to an engineer and it just actually works. That's what's insane about this. And so that's why this example you're sharing of go-to-market folks, building their own things, it's like they don't need to know anything about product building. It's just describe it in some ridiculous way and draw a couple boxes of what you want it to look like and it makes something for you.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得很酷的是，当你回看最初的演示片段时，基本上就是产品经理对工程师说：“嘿，给我开发一个面向狗狗的Airbnb吧。这是我用几个盒子做的粗糙模型。”这简直就像一个糟糕的产品经理对工程师说话，但最后居然成功了。这才是最不可思议的地方。所以你分享的那些市场团队自主开发产品的例子，他们甚至不需要懂产品开发。他们只需用某种夸张的方式描述需求，画几个盒子示意功能，就能为你创造出东西。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Which shows that agency is what matters. If you have a product manager that has an idea, there's no reason for why that idea cannot be more well fleshed out. How many times do you have a product manager that just continualize ideas, but it just feels like they are extremely unsure on how to execute on it? They just want to say things for sake of saying things? But for the people that have ideas and a lot of, I guess, agency, they can go out and prove out what they want without any sort of external resources.
turns.zh: 这表明自主权至关重要。如果有一个产品经理有想法，根本没有理由不把这个想法完善得更充分。有多少产品经理只是不断重复同样的想法，却让人感觉他们对如何执行毫无头绪？他们只是为了说话而说话？但对于那些有想法且有足够自主权的人来说，他们可以利用现有资源去验证自己的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think even more acutely for product folks listening to this, it's the salesperson coming to you being like, "Hey, I want this thing. It's going to help me with my sales team." And you're like, "I don't have a million things to build. I don't have time for this." And so that problem goes away, which I think will make a lot of product leaders really happy. (00:54:04): The model that this is sitting on, is it Sonnet?
turns.zh: 我想对于听众中的产品人员来说，更尖锐的问题是，销售人员会来找你说：“嘿，我想要这个工具，它能帮我提升销售团队的效率。”而你会说：“我手头要做的事已经够多了，没时间搞这个。”但现在这个问题迎刃而解了，我觉得这会让很多产品负责人非常高兴。（00:54:04）：这个模型所基于的框架，是Sonnet吗？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah. So just to break down how it ultimately works, we have a model that does planning. And I would say right now Sonnet is a really, really good planning model. I think OpenAI's GPT-4o is also good. But the crazy thing is what we try to do is we try to make the Anthropic based model or Sonnet model try to do as much of the high level planning as possible. And then what we try to do internally is run all the models necessary to do high quality retrieval for the agent. As you could see, the agent needed to understand what the rest of the code base ultimately did. We actually make sure we run models to actually chunk up the entire code base and understand the code base so that obviously it would not be a good idea if we had a 100 million line code base to send that entire code base to Anthropic. (00:54:49): First of all, you couldn't do that. That's over 1.5 billion tokens of code. So obviously that would be three or four orders of my actually larger than the largest context lens right now. (00:54:58): But you also wouldn't want to do that from a cost and latency standpoint too. So that's one. And the second piece that you saw was the model is able to very quickly make edits to the software as well. We have custom models that we built that are post trained on top of popular open source models that can make these edits really, really quickly to the code base. And the reason why you would want to do that is it's A, faster, and B, also that model can actually have more of the code base in context too. So it can be better at applying changes than even Anthropics model too. (00:55:28): So I think the way we like to think about it is, our only goal is how do we build the best product possible? How do we build the best product possible and how do we make the ceiling as high as possible? And we will go out and build models and train models wherever necessary. But if we're not going to be good at a task and we think the open source is better or Anthropic's better, we'll go and just use the open source or Anthropic.
turns.zh: 是的。简单说一下它的运作原理，我们有一个用于规划的模型。我得说目前Sonnet确实是个非常出色的规划模型。OpenAI的GPT-4也是不错的。但关键在于，我们试图让基于Anthropic的模型或Sonnet模型尽可能多地完成高层规划任务。然后我们内部会运行所有必要的模型，为智能体提供高质量的检索功能。正如你所见，智能体需要理解代码库的整体结构。我们确保运行模型来分割整个代码库并理解其内容——毕竟如果要把一个1亿行的代码库全部发送给Anthropic，那显然是不可行的。（00:54:49）：首先，你根本做不到。代码量超过15亿个token。显然这比目前最大的上下文窗口大三个或四个数量级。（00:54:58）：而且从成本和延迟角度来看，你也不想这么做。这是第一点。第二点你看到的是模型能够快速对软件进行编辑。我们开发了定制模型，这些模型在流行开源模型的基础上进行了额外训练，能够极快地对代码库进行编辑。这样做的原因在于：A，更快；B，模型也能更好地理解整个代码库的上下文。因此，它在应用更改方面比Anthropic的模型表现更出色。（00:55:28）：所以我们倾向于这样思考：我们的唯一目标是如何打造出尽可能优秀的产品？如何打造出尽可能优秀的产品，并将上限设得尽可能高？我们会去开发和训练模型，只要有必要。但如果我们在某项任务上不擅长，而开源工具或Anthropic的模型更胜一筹，我们就会毫不犹豫地选择后者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so the models you guys are building, those are built on open source models that people are releasing?
turns.zh: 那么你们开发的这些模型，是基于开源模型构建的吗？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah. Interestingly, the one that does retrieval is actually completely pre-trained in-house that actually does that. But yeah, for a lot of different pieces, it's based on open source. Interestingly for the one that does the edits and auto-complete, that is also in-house. As you're typing, we actually do some auto-complete related stuff. I'm happy to show that, but I think a lot of users are familiar with that capability. So I think the way we like to look at it is like, what could we be best at and we will go out and trade. But if we're not going to be best at it, we should not just, for the sake of ego, go out and trade something.
turns.zh: 是的。有趣的是，用于检索的模型实际上是在内部完全预训练好的，但其他许多模块都是基于开源的。有趣的是，用于编辑和自动补全的模型也是内部开发的。当你输入代码时，我们会进行一些自动补全相关的操作。我很乐意展示这一功能，但我认为很多用户对这项功能已经很熟悉了。所以我们的看法是，专注于我们最擅长的领域，必要时进行合作。但如果我们不擅长某项任务，就不应该为了面子而强行合作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This may be getting too technical, but just, is there anything interesting around what you train on?
turns.zh: 这可能有点技术性了，但你能谈谈你们训练模型的数据吗？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah, so one of the interesting things that we have from our users, and this is where we try to think like, "Why would we be any better?" is that, actually every hour, we get probably tens of millions of pieces of feedback from our users. We get a lot of feedback on what they like and what they don't like. For something like autocomplete, we get a lot of preference data, a lot of preference data. And the preference data is weird. It doesn't look like data that you find on the internet. It's like data as the user is typing. Imagine you're typing some code in a code base, the code's going to be incomplete as you're typing it, right? It's not going to be in a full-fledged form. It's not like it is on GitHub. But we have a lot of data that looks like this. (00:57:06): So we are uniquely well-positioned to actually build a good model that can complete code even when it's in an incomplete state when the models that are out there, the frontier models have consumed very little code that looks like this. So for that case we're like, "Hey, we can go out and do a much better job potentially." And we'll go out and train models on all the preference data we have. (00:57:25): The same is kind of true on retrieval, right? There's a way to find out, are we retrieving the right data? Did the user accept the code change after that? Was the retrieval actually a good retrieval a signal that we can get? So basically the way we like to look at it is, if something is just purely code planning, there's not a great reason why we would be the best at that. I can't come up with a coherent argument for that. But for something that looks more along the lines of, "Hey, here's an intermediate code base that is very gnarly and here are some changes that need to get made" and we know the evolution of the code or we've seen the evolution of code across millions of users, we feel like we can do a great job of that.
turns.zh: 是的，用户反馈给我们的一些有趣之处——这也是我们试图思考“我们凭什么能做得更好？”的时候——是这样的，实际上每小时我们就能收到数千万条用户反馈。我们收到大量关于用户喜欢什么、不喜欢什么的反馈。对于自动补全功能，我们收集了大量偏好数据，非常多的偏好数据。这些偏好数据很特别，不像你在网上能找到的数据。它们就像用户正在输入代码时的数据。想象你正在代码库中输入一些代码，代码在你输入时是不完整的，对吧？它不会是完整的形式，不像在GitHub上的那样。但我们有很多类似这样的数据。（00:57:06）：所以我们处于独特的有利位置，可以真正构建一个即使在代码不完整时也能完成补全的模型，而现有的前沿模型很少处理这种类型的数据。因此，在这种情况下，我们会想，“嘿，我们可以出去做得更好。”我们会利用我们拥有的所有偏好数据来训练模型。（00:57:25）：检索功能方面也是如此，对吧？有办法验证我们是否检索到了正确的数据？用户在那之后是否接受了代码更改？检索是否确实是一个好的检索，是否是一个我们能获取的信号？所以基本上，我们的看法是，如果这只是纯粹的代码规划，就没有什么理由我们能在这方面做到最好。对于这类事情，我想不出一个连贯的论点。但对于看起来更像是，“嘿，这里有一个非常复杂的中间代码库，需要进行一些更改”这样的情况，我们知道代码的演变，或者我们已经见证了数百万用户的代码演变，我们觉得我们能在这方面做得很出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think what's interesting about this is another differentiator/moat for companies that end up winning in this space, is you just have more and more of that data than other companies if you're ahead.
turns.zh: 我认为有趣的是，对于最终在这个领域胜出的公司来说，另一个差异化因素/护城河是，如果你领先，你就能比其他公司拥有更多这样的数据。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah. This is sort of why maybe at a high level we like the zero-to-one app building product space. I think it's really... It's a good product space. But ultimately I think it needs to boil down to you understanding the code, because otherwise, you're living at too high a plane where it's not clear why you would be able to be the best at that compared to everyone else. It's not really clear.
turns.zh: 是的。这就是为什么从高层来看，我们喜欢零到一的应用构建产品领域。我认为这确实是一个不错的产品领域。但最终，我认为这必须归结到你对代码的理解上，因为否则，你就生活在一个太高的层面上，很难清楚为什么你能在这方面比其他人做得更好。真的不清楚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As a company, you mean?
turns.zh: 作为一家公司，你的意思是？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: As a company.
turns.zh: 作为一家公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Versus as a user.
turns.zh: 而不是作为用户。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: It feels like it might get competitive in a way that it's not clear where you would continue to differentiate over and over with time.
turns.zh: 感觉它可能会变得竞争激烈，以至于不清楚你如何能随着时间不断进行差异化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. Because if they're just sitting on top of Sonnet and just doing what every other Sonnet wrapper is doing, there's not a lot of differentiation or moat.
turns.zh: 我明白了。因为如果他们只是基于Sonnet，然后做其他Sonnet包装器都在做的事情，那就没有太多的差异化或护城河了。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: It depends on how you do it. But maybe if I was to say this, if the inputs you're consuming are just web elements, extremely high level web elements, then the interface might be high level enough that it's hard to maybe get better than maybe what the frontier models are doing just across the board. You are just better off just plugging in Sonnet for everything.
turns.zh: 这取决于你如何操作。但或许我要说的是，如果你所使用的输入只是网页元素——极其高级的网页元素——那么界面可能足够高级，以至于很难超越前沿模型目前的水平。你最好还是直接使用Sonnet来处理所有需求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Awesome. One thing I wanted to come back to that I wrote down that I think is really important for people to understand, you talked about how with Windsurf it's not necessarily... There's a boilerplate code base that you want to start with because it's actually... Because it's not an abstracted zero-to-one app builder. It's an actual IDE you're coding in. And you talked about how has to install dependencies, which is kind this painful thing. And the reason it has to do that is because running locally on your machine versus in the cloud, like, say, Lovable and Replit and all these guys, although I think Bolt runs in your browser in this really cool way. (00:59:47): So that's an important distinction. This is like you're running this locally in your machine and has all the libraries you need to actually run it.
turns.zh: 明白了。太棒了。我还想回顾一下我之前记下的一点，我认为这对大家理解很重要。你提到Windsurf不一定……你需要从一个模板化的代码库入手，因为它实际上……它不是一个抽象的零到一的应用生成器。它是一个你实际编码的IDE。你还谈到必须安装依赖项，这确实很麻烦。而必须这样做的原因是，在本地机器上运行与在云端运行不同，比如Lovable、Replit等平台，不过我认为Bolt在浏览器中以一种非常酷的方式运行。（00:59:47）：所以这是一个重要的区别。这就像你在本地机器上运行它，拥有实际运行它所需的所有库。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: No, I think that's important. I think we believe a lot of people sort of build software in what are called code spaces and things in a remote machine. I just think it's that a lot of developers like building locally for what you said. Like if you're doing things that are more than just full stack applications, you might have dependencies on your machine that are just system dependencies that are just gnarly to install. Let's imagine you're building a GPU-based application and the Nvidia drivers, they're necessary. You just want to give people the flexibility to build where they can build. And I think the IDE and building locally has been a thing that people have done for decades, so probably it's not going to go away in the next couple of years.
turns.zh: 不，我认为这很重要。我们相信很多开发者在远程机器上的代码空间等环境中构建软件。我只是觉得很多开发者喜欢在本地构建，正如你所说。如果你正在做的事情不仅仅是全栈应用，你的机器上可能有一些依赖项，这些依赖项很难安装。想象一下你正在构建一个基于GPU的应用，而Nvidia驱动程序是必需的。你只是想给人们在能构建的地方构建的灵活性。我认为IDE和本地构建几十年来一直是开发者常用的，所以在未来几年内它不太可能消失。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that your sales folks now are running local host servers.
turns.zh: 我很高兴你们的销售人员现在正在运行本地主机服务器。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Well, with the browser previews, it's easier, right? You kind of just open it up on the side.
turns.zh: 嗯，使用浏览器预览更容易，对吧？你只需在侧边栏打开它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Oh my god. Okay. I have a few more questions just about how you think and operate at Codeium. So you guys are kind of at the forefront of how product teams are going to operate. You're seeing the future every day. And so I'm curious if there's ways you guys have structured your teams, engineers, product design that might be different from how other companies are doing it or have tried stuff that has worked really well or tried stuff that's a huge disaster?
turns.zh: 是的。是的。天哪。好的。我还有几个关于你们在Codeium如何思考和运作的问题。所以你们处于产品团队运作方式的前沿。你们每天都在见证未来。所以我很好奇你们是否以某种方式构建了团队、工程师、产品设计，可能与其他公司不同，或者尝试过非常有效的方法，或者尝试过巨大的灾难？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: One interesting decision that we kind of have for core engineering is that we don't have pure product managers for the core engineering side of the company. And by the way, that's purely because we build for developers and our product is built by developers. So I think the intuition from our own developers is hopefully valuable. If not, we might be hiring the wrong type of people. So I think our developers are, in some sense, flexing to be more product conventional product managers. (01:01:32): Now on the other hand, if we were building something that looked more like Uber or the persona was very different and we didn't ourselves understand it, I think the organization wouldn't look the way it looks. (01:01:42): For the enterprise side of the company, because we do work with a lot of large enterprises where the requirements are not something that our engineers would automatically understand, I don't think our engineers wake up and they're like, "We need FedRAMP." This is probably something that a lot of customers come to us with and tell us. We have people that flex in this product strategy role that understand what the customer wants and understands the technical capabilities that we have to best build a product that would help them at scale. (01:02:12): So I think we have an interesting organization in this regard, but mostly I would say because we are a developer-based product, I would say that's true. (01:02:21): And then also kind of like what you said for the engineering team itself, the team structure is, it's fairly flat. We try to go with two pizza teams, teams that are fairly small just because I think the problem is when a team gets too big, the person leading the team is no longer able to get in the weeds of the technology itself. And I think in a space that's moving this quickly, I think it's dangerous to have leaders that don't understand the technology deeply and are not building. It's very, very dangerous because there's too much armchair quarterbacking. And so I think that's maybe one other decision we made. (01:02:56): And then teams are very, very flexible. So if we decide something is a new priority, we're very quick to change the way a team looks. And it's very centrally planned in this regard.
turns.zh:
关于核心工程团队，我们做出的一个有趣决策是，我们的公司内部没有纯粹的产品经理。这完全是因为我们为开发者服务，我们的产品也是由开发者打造的。所以我认为，我们开发者提出的见解应该是有价值的。如果不是这样，那我们可能就招错人了。所以我觉得我们的开发者在某种程度上正在灵活地转型为更传统的产品经理。（01:01:32）  
但另一方面，如果我们要开发的产品更像优步（Uber），或者用户需求与我们的工程师自身理解相差甚远，那公司的组织架构可能就不会是现在这个样子了。（01:01:42）  
对于企业业务线，因为我们与许多大型企业合作，他们的需求并非我们的工程师能轻易理解的。我认为我们的工程师不会一觉醒来就说：“我们需要FedRAMP认证。”这很可能是许多客户向我们提出并告知我们的需求。我们有专门负责产品策略的团队，他们了解客户需求，理解我们现有的技术能力，从而能以最佳方式打造出能大规模助力客户的解决方案。（01:02:12）  
所以我认为我们在这方面有一个有趣的组织架构，但最重要的是，因为我们是以开发者为核心的产品公司，所以我认为这确实如此。（01:02:21）  
再说回工程团队本身，团队结构相当扁平。我们尝试采用两个“披萨团队”模式，团队规模较小，因为我认为当团队规模过大时，团队负责人就无法深入钻研技术本身了。在快速发展的领域中，如果领导者不深入理解技术且不亲自参与开发，那是十分危险的，因为这会导致他们只会纸上谈兵。所以我认为这或许是我们做出的另一个决策。（01:02:56）  
然后团队的灵活性极强。如果我们决定将某项工作列为新优先级，我们就能迅速调整团队结构。在这方面，我们的规划是集中化的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The two pizza team concept, I saw a tweet long ago where someone from India, was like, there's always talk about two pizza teams, but pizzas in India are much smaller. And so the teams end up being smaller and they're like, "Why can't we build as much of these teams in the US?"
turns.zh: 关于两个披萨团队的概念，我很久以前看到过一条推文，印度有人说，人们总是在谈论两个披萨团队，但印度的披萨份量小得多。所以团队规模也更小，他们还问：“为什么我们在美国就不能组建更多这样的团队呢？”

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Oh man.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So how many PMs do you have? So you said you have 150 employees, something like that?
turns.zh: 好的。那你们有多少个产品经理？你说你们有150名员工，差不多是这个数吧？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah. So in terms of the product strategy function, we have three people in that role right now.
turns.zh: 对。就产品策略职能而言，目前我们有三个人负责这个角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. So it's like product... They're in their titles is product strategy, not necessarily product management?
turns.zh: 我明白了。所以他们的职位名称是产品策略，而不是产品管理？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. And then 50 engineers, you said 80-ish sales folks?
turns.zh: 有意思。然后有50名工程师，你说大约80名销售人员？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yes, that's right. And then obviously we have functions like recruiting parts of G&A, like finance. We have marketing at the company. So some other functions internally as well.
turns.zh: 对，没错。然后还有一些其他职能部门，比如招聘、行政、财务、市场部等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting. And this is something that you hear all the time with companies like Dario for example, from Anthropic talking about how 90% of code is going to be written by AI. But all at the same time, all you guys are hiring engineers like crazy.
turns.zh: 真有意思。像达里奥这样的公司，还有Anthropic，总是声称90%的代码将由AI编写。但与此同时，大家却还在疯狂招聘工程师。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah. Is that contradictory?
turns.zh: 是啊。这难道不矛盾吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's that contradictory, will there be an inflection point of like, "All right. Now we don't need them anymore."
turns.zh: 确实矛盾啊，会不会到某个临界点时，人们就会说：“好吧，我们现在不需要他们了。”

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: I think it really comes down to, do you get incremental value by adding more engineers internally? I'm going to take... First of all, maybe just to set the record straight, if AI is writing over 90% of the code, that doesn't mean engineers are 10X as productive. Engineers spend more time than just writing code. The review code, test code, debug code, design code, deploy code, right? Navigate code. There's probably a lot of different things that engineers do. There's this one famous law in parallel computing, it's called Amdahl's Law. I don't know if you've heard about it. But it basically says if you have a graph of tasks and you have this critical path and you take any one task and parallelize it a ton, which is make it almost take zero amount of time, there's still a limit of the amount of how much faster it made the whole process go. (01:04:56): So maybe put simply, let's say you have 100 units of time and only 30 units of time is being spent writing software and I took the 30 and made it three, I only took the 100 and made it 73. It's only a 27% improvement in the grand scheme of things. (01:05:09): So I think look, we are definitely seeing over 30, maybe close to 40% productivity improvements. But I think for the vision that we're solving for, even if I were to say the company in the long tail had 200 engineers, it'd probably be too low still at that point. So the question is, how much more productivity do you get per person? Actually, maybe just to even say one of those thing for some of these large companies, let's say you took the CIO of a company like JPMorgan Chase, right? Her budget on software every year is $17 billion and there's over 50,000 engineers inside the company and you told her, "Hey, each of these engineers are now able to produce more technology." That's effectively what you've done, right? The right calculus that JPMorgan Chase or any of these companies will make is the ROI of building technology has actually gone up. So the opportunity cost of not investing more into technology has gone up, which means that you should just invest even more. And maybe in the short term you have even more engineers, right? (01:06:08): Now, that's not true across the board. There are some companies that are happy with the amount of technology they're building and there's a ceiling on the amount of technology they want to build. But for companies that actually have a very high technology ceiling, this doesn't mean you stop. This actually means you hire more.
turns.zh: 我觉得关键在于，内部增加工程师能带来多少增量价值？首先，可能需要澄清一下，如果AI能编写90%的代码，这并不意味着工程师的生产力提高了10倍。工程师的工作远不止编写代码——他们还要进行代码审查、测试、调试、设计、部署，以及导航代码等工作。并行计算领域有著名的阿姆达尔定律，不知道你们是否听说过。简单来说，如果有任务图，其中存在关键路径，而你将某个任务大量并行化（让其耗时接近零），最终整体进程的加速效果依然有限。（01:04:56）：打个比方，假设你有100个工作单位，其中30个用于编写软件，我把这30个压缩到3个单位，总工作量不变，但只剩下73个单位，增益只有27%。（01:05:09）：所以我们确实看到了30%甚至接近40%的生产力提升。但从长远目标来看，哪怕一家拥有200名工程师的大公司，产能提升空间可能还是太小了。关键在于，每个工程师能多产出多少价值？以摩根大通这样的公司为例，CIO每年在软件上的预算达170亿美元，公司内部有5万多名工程师。如果你告诉她：“现在每个工程师都能产出更多技术成果。”这实际上就是你在做的事，对吧？摩根大通或其他公司会计算，开发技术的投资回报率实际上已经提高了。因此，不投入更多技术的机会成本也随之上升，这意味着你应该加大投入。短期内可能工程师数量会增加，对吧？（01:06:08）：但并非所有公司都如此。有些公司对现有技术产出很满意，或者对技术产出设有上限。但对于那些技术上限很高的公司来说，这并不意味着停下脚步，而是意味着继续招聘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a great bull case for engineers. I feel like the canary in the coal mine for the engineering profession is when companies like yours slow down on hiring engineers.
turns.zh: 这对工程师来说是个绝佳的利好案例。我觉得工程师行业的预警信号就是像你们这样的公司放缓招聘工程师的步伐。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's not happening.
turns.zh: 但这种情况并未发生。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: [inaudible 01:06:32]. It seems like Anthropic is also hiring a lot to get it done.
turns.zh: [01:06:32不可听清]。看起来Anthropic也在大量招聘以完成任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Everyone is. So I think that's really promising. I think if you're in college still, makes sense to get into engineering at this point. (01:06:40): Okay. Let me ask you this question as kind of a final question maybe. What's maybe the most counterintuitive thing you've learned about building AI products, building Windsurf and just being in a space?
turns.zh: 是啊，每个人都是这样。所以我觉得这真的很振奋人心。如果你还在上大学，现在转入工程领域还是很明智的。（01:06:40）：好的。让我问你最后一个问题吧。你在开发人工智能产品、打造Windsurf以及整个行业中，有没有学到什么最违背直觉的东西？

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: I think one of the weird things is online, everyone is very excited about the short-term wins that we are making, right? Like what we're putting out maybe weekly. We do these waves every couple of weeks. But actually a lot of the bets we're making inside the company are for things that are not three, four weeks, maybe three, six months, nine months away. That's what we're working on internally. Because I think this is kind of, Lenny, what I was mentioning to you before. One of the goals that I tell everyone at our company is we should be cannibalizing the existing state of our product every six to 12 months. Every six to 12 months, it should make our existing product look silly. It should almost make the form factor of our existing product look dumb. (01:07:31): So there's this weird tension where you want to have a product in market and you want to incrementally iterate and listen to users and keep making it better and better. But I would say we were the first identical IDE product out there. That's what we landed with. And I think the value of that is going to depreciate very quickly unless we continue to re-prove ourselves. And we will need to re-prove ourselves in ways in which our users are not even asking. So there's this tension here, where incremental feels very safe, right? Add this one more button. Users say, "Hey, I would like to be able to have this drop down to do X." But that is not the reason why we're going to win. That's almost table sticks. Yeah, we'll decide to do some of these. We might not decide to do a lot of these things. But it's these longer term efforts inside the company that almost disrupt the existing product that are ultimately the reason why we're going to succeed. (01:08:21): It's this weird tension that you need to have in your head of, you can't also not listen to your users at all because they're the reason you exist.
turns.zh: 我觉得其中一个奇怪之处在于，网上所有人都对我们短期取得的成果感到兴奋，对吧？比如我们每周发布的产品，每隔几周就会推出新版本。但实际上，我们公司内部做的大多数决策，涉及的产品改进周期都不是三四周，而是三六个月、九个月。这些才是我们内部正在努力的方向。因为我觉得，莱尼，我之前跟你提到的这一点很重要。我告诉公司里的每个人：我们每六到十二个月就应该对现有产品进行彻底革新。每六到十二个月，我们的现有产品就应该显得过时。它甚至应该让现有产品的形态显得愚蠢。（01:07:31）：所以这里存在一种奇怪的矛盾：你既想让产品上市，又想不断迭代、倾听用户反馈、让产品越来越好。但我要说的是，我们当时是市面上首款完全相同的IDE产品。这就是我们当时推出的产品。我认为它的价值很快就会贬值，除非我们不断重新证明自己的价值。我们需要以用户甚至都想不到的方式来证明自己。所以这里存在一种矛盾：渐进式改进看似安全，对吧？比如增加一个按钮。用户会说：“嘿，我希望能有个下拉菜单来做X。”但这不是我们取胜的关键。这几乎是无关痛痒的改进。我们可能会决定做其中一些改进，但也可能决定不做很多。但公司内部这些长期努力，几乎是在颠覆现有产品，这才是我们最终成功的关键。

turns.en: This reminds me of a recent podcast guest. We had Gara from captions on the podcast and he told us that he has two roadmaps. They have two roadmaps at the company. turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I love that he calls it the secret roadmap just to make it very mysterious and-

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: That's smarts. That's very smart.
turns.zh: 这很聪明。非常聪明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I have one more question. I apologize. What's one thing that you wish he had known before starting Codeium?

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Honestly, I wish I had... Maybe humility is the wrong term, but this idea of just being okay with being wrong faster. I always think about things on when we make decisions. Me and my co-founder, we always talk about it. We're almost like, "Hey, I wish we had made the decision to do this a couple months earlier." We always talk about this. And the weird thing is outside looking and everyone's like, "Wow, actually the decision was made at the right time." But in my head I'm always banging my head being like, "What if we had made it a couple months earlier?" I think part of that is I waxed poetically about like, "Oh, you need to be irrationally optimistic and uncompromisingly realistic." But it's very hard to do this in practice because you drink your own Kool-Aid too. Because if you're not drinking your own, you won't get up out of bed. The answer is already solved. It's not actually any of these startups. The answer is Microsoft is going to be the winner in any software category. Isn't that the answer? Just because of distribution, resources and capital, they're going to commoditize every space. (01:10:06): So I think in some ways this amount of just understanding that, hey, re-evaluate your hypotheses and get into an uncomfortable space way more frequently is something I need to remind myself even to this day. And probably something that I didn't know coming in and starting the company. We started the company at peak zero time. At that time, probably everything seemed like it was going to moon. And there was probably a lot of irrational confidence, I would say, that we shouldn't have had.
turns.zh: 老实说，我真希望当时能……或许“谦逊”这个词用得不太恰当，但我指的是能更坦然地接受自己犯错的现实。每当我们做决策时，我和我的联合创始人总会反复讨论这件事。我们常感慨：“唉，真希望我们能早几个月就做出这个决定。”这种讨论频率很高。但外界看来，大家都会惊叹：“哇，你们这个决定真是选对了时机！”而我却总在心里反复追问：“要是早几个月行动会怎样？” 我觉得部分原因在于，我曾高谈阔论过“要保持非理性乐观，坚持现实主义”之类的话。但在实践中，这太难了。因为你也会被自己的偏见所束缚——若不这样，你根本起不了床。答案早已注定。真正能获胜的并非这些初创公司，而是微软。只要看其分销渠道、资源和资金实力，微软就能将任何软件领域标准化。（01:10:06）所以我觉得，在某种程度上，要明白并经常重新评估自己的假设，勇于面对不确定性，才是我至今仍需要时刻提醒自己的关键。而这在创办公司之初，我或许并未意识到这一点。我们创办公司时正值行业寒冬。彼时，一切似乎都注定要飞黄腾达。人们可能充满了不切实际的自信，而这份自信本不该存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And when you say get your hands dirty, basically it's like download Windsurf, start coding. Ask it to build things for you.
turns.zh: 你说的亲自实践，基本就是下载Windsurf，开始编码。让它为你构建代码。

turns.speaker: Varun Mohan
turns.en: Yeah, build apps. Build apps. Start using it for maybe even making mocks, modifying your existing code base. Imagine if you were a product manager that could actually very quickly make edits to the code base and just start pushing changes yourself. turns.en: Yeah.
